title: Rigidification detects categorical equivalences
statement: Use simplicial sets [def-weil-pbc-simplicial-set], simplicial categories as defined in [lem-coef-simplicial-interval-lifting], and categorical equivalences in the testing convention of [lem-coef-joyal-model-structure]: $f:S\to T$ is such an equivalence when $h\operatorname{Fun}(T,Z)\to h\operatorname{Fun}(S,Z)$ is an equivalence for every quasicategory $Z$ in a sufficiently large universe. For $n\geq0$, define $\mathfrak C[\Delta^n]$ with objects $0,\ldots,n$ and mapping simplicial set from $i$ to $j$ for $i\leq j$ the ordinary nerve of the poset of subsets of $\{i,\ldots,j\}$ containing both endpoints, ordered by inclusion; the mapping set is empty for $i>j$. Composition is union of subsets. A monotone map induces the enriched functor given by image of subsets. For every simplicial set $S$, put $\mathfrak C[S]=\operatorname{colim}_{\Delta^n\to S}\mathfrak C[\Delta^n]$, with colimit in $\mathrm{sCat}$. Then for every simplicial map $f:S\to T$, $\mathfrak C[f]$ is a Dwyer--Kan equivalence [lem-coef-simplicial-interval-cell-stability] if and only if $f$ is a categorical equivalence.

source.place: Theorem 2.2.5.1, condition (W), and Proposition 2.2.5.8 (the homotopy-category-of-functors test). No Stacks tag states this rigidification criterion.

proof.text: Write $\mathfrak C$ for the construction in the statement. Cocompleteness of $\mathrm{sCat}$ gives its simplex colimits. Define $N(A)_n=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{sCat}}(\mathfrak C[\Delta^n],A)$, with operators by precomposition. A simplicial map $S\to N(A)$ is exactly a compatible family of enriched functors on the simplices of $S$, so the colimit universal property gives $\mathfrak C\dashv N$; in particular $\mathfrak C$ preserves colimits. There is also a natural identity-on-objects isomorphism $\pi_0\mathfrak C[S]\cong hS$. Indeed enriched functors $\mathfrak C[S]\to D$, for an ordinary category $D$ regarded as discretely enriched, factor uniquely through $\pi_0\mathfrak C[S]$. On a simplex the subset-poset nerves are connected for $i\leq j$, giving $\pi_0\mathfrak C[\Delta^n]=[n]$. Consequently such functors are compatible functors $[n]\to D$ on all simplices of $S$: they assign arrows to edges, identities to degenerate edges, and the composition relation to every triangle, which is precisely the presentation of $hS$ in the Joyal input. The resulting isomorphism sends a vertex to that vertex and commutes with every simplicial map.

source.place: Section 1.1.5 (coherent realization and nerve); definition of hS; simplex-colimit universal property

proof.text:
For $n\geq2$ and $0<i<n$, compute the realization of the inner horn inclusion. Both enriched categories have objects $0,\ldots,n$, and their mapping sets agree except from $0$ to $n$. Put $B=(\Delta^1)^{n-1}$, with coordinate $t_j$ recording membership of the intermediate vertex $j$ in a subset. The exceptional mapping inclusion is $K\hookrightarrow B$, where
$$K=\bigcup_{1\leq j<n}\{t_j=1\}\ \cup\ \bigcup_{1\leq j<n,\ j\ne i}\{t_j=0\}.$$
To see this directly from the colimit presentation, omitting an intermediate vertex $j\ne i$ gives the face $t_j=0$; composing through an intermediate vertex $j$ gives $t_j=1$, since union of subsets is composition. Each factor of such a composition belongs to a proper interval contained in an allowed horn face. These exhaust the generators of the horn colimit; their overlaps impose exactly the common-face identifications. The proper intervals give unchanged mapping sets. Thus $\mathfrak C[\Lambda_i^n]\to\mathfrak C[\Delta^n]$ is a pushout of $U(K)\to U(B)$ along the functor selecting $0,n$. The current realization theorem preserves finite products in $\mathcal K$, so $|B|$ is the product of the realized intervals. Its finite-limit clause identifies intersections of these coordinate faces, and its small-colimit clause identifies their union: add faces successively by the pushout of their intersection with the union already formed. These colimits in $\mathcal K$ are the topological colimits. Each coordinate face and each intersection is a compact closed subspace of the finite cube. The union has the final topology for its finitely many closed faces: a subset is closed exactly when its intersections with all the faces are closed, since the union is finite. Thus the successive topological pushouts give exactly the displayed union with its subspace topology. In the realized cube, increasing coordinate $t_i$ linearly to $1$ is a deformation retraction of $|K|$ onto the face $t_i=1$; that face is a cube. Contract that face to its all-ones vertex and contract the entire cube $|B|$ to the same vertex. The constant map $|B|\to|K|$ at that vertex is thus an inverse to the inclusion up to continuous homotopies. By [lem-coef-homotopy-groups-basepoint-change], this homotopy equivalence induces bijections on path components and isomorphisms on all homotopy groups at every basepoint. Therefore $K\hookrightarrow B$ is a monomorphism and a weak homotopy equivalence, hence a Kan--Quillen trivial cofibration. The horn-retract description in the Kan--Quillen input expresses it as a retract of a relative horn-cell map. Applying $U$ expresses $U(K)\to U(B)$ as a retract of attachments of the enriched horn maps in $J$: at every attachment there are just the fixed two objects and the indicated mapping set, so the fixed-object pushouts have exactly the original simplicial pushout as their $0$-to-$1$ mapping set. Hence the enriched inner-horn inclusion belongs to $J\text{-cof}$. For $n=2$, $K$ is the endpoint $1$ of $\Delta^1$; there are no inner horns in dimensions $0,1$.

source.place: Lemma 2.2.5.2, explicit inner-horn cube calculation; elementary deformation of the cube

proof.text: It follows that $\mathfrak C$ sends every inner-horn-cell map to $J\text{-cof}$. Here an inner-horn-cell map is a transfinite composite of pushouts of coproducts of inner horn inclusions. Indeed step 1 preserves all these colimits, and left lifting against $J\text{-inj}$ is preserved by these operations: extend the filler over each attached cell and at a limit take the compatible colimit of the earlier fillers. Retracts preserve lifting by composing with their section and retraction. By the interval-lifting input every $J\text{-cof}$ map is a retract of a $J\text{-cell}$ map. Interval-cell stability and retract closure therefore show that $\mathfrak C$ sends all inner-horn-cell maps, and their retracts, to Dwyer--Kan equivalences. This argument makes no local Kan assumption on the intermediate enriched categories.

source.place: Lemma 2.2.5.2, weak saturation argument, using the existing enriched small-object and cell-stability statements

proof.text: Apply the functorial cellular small-object factorization to the maps $S\to\Delta^0$ and $T\to\Delta^0$, using the set of inner horn inclusions. Simplicial colimits are degreewise set colimits, and each horn has finitely many nondegenerate simplices, so every map from a horn into a sequential union of these monomorphisms factors through a finite stage, with equalities also detected at a finite stage. Thus the smallness hypothesis holds with the regular cardinal $\omega$. Obtain functorial inner-horn-cell inclusions $r_S:S\to S'$ and $r_T:T\to T'$ and a commutative square $r_T f=f' r_S$. The maps from $S',T'$ to the point lift all inner horns, so $S',T'$ are quasicategories. Inner horn inclusions are Joyal trivial cofibrations by the Joyal input. Their cell maps are trivial cofibrations as well: lift against any Joyal fibration cell by cell and use the weak factorization system. Hence $r_S,r_T$ are categorical equivalences in the testing convention, and step 3 shows that $\mathfrak C[r_S],\mathfrak C[r_T]$ are Dwyer--Kan equivalences. All attachments, including their indexing sets, stay in the original universe; only the testing categories may require the larger universe already specified in the item.

source.place: Proof of Theorem 2.2.5.1, inner-anodyne replacement; explicit small-object construction with the existing factorization theorem

proof.text: Now consider a map $g:A\to B$ between quasicategories. For each $x,y\in A_0$ the pinched-resolution input supplies a commutative square with vertical weak homotopy equivalences $\theta_{A,x,y}$ and $\theta_{B,gx,gy}$, upper horizontal map $|\operatorname{Map}^R_A(x,y)|_Q\to|\operatorname{Map}^R_B(gx,gy)|_Q$, and lower horizontal map $\mathfrak C[g]_{x,y}$. Its natural weak equivalences $p_M:|M|_Q\to M$ give a second commutative square comparing the upper horizontal map with $\operatorname{Map}^R_A(x,y)\to\operatorname{Map}^R_B(gx,gy)$. Two-out-of-three in the Kan--Quillen model structure shows that the lower horizontal map is a weak homotopy equivalence exactly when the right-mapping-space map is one. If this holds for all $x,y$, the functor $\pi_0\mathfrak C[g]$ is already fully faithful, so it is an equivalence exactly when it is essentially surjective. By the natural isomorphism of step 1 the latter condition is essential surjectivity of $hg$. Thus $\mathfrak C[g]$ is Dwyer--Kan exactly when $g$ is weakly equivalent on every right mapping space and $hg$ is essentially surjective. Only here, after replacement, do we apply the comparison that requires quasicategories.

source.place: Propositions 2.2.4.1 and 2.2.2.7; natural pinched mapping-space comparison, with the component-category identification of step 1

proof.text: Under the two conditions at the end of step 5, $g$ is fully faithful in the right-mapping-space convention. Let $B_0$ be its full replete essential image. Apply [lem-coef-infinity-full-essential-image] to obtain a coherent inverse to $g:A\to B_0$. Essential surjectivity of $hg$ says that every vertex of $B$ is isomorphic in $hB$ to some $g(x)$, hence equivalent to $g(x)$ in the quasicategory convention. Here, for a quasicategory $\mathcal D$, the generated category $h\mathcal D$ of the Joyal input is identified with the category of [lem-coef-infinity-mapping-composition] by the identity on vertices and edges: the latter respects degenerate edges and $2$-simplex relations by that node, it is full because every component is represented by an edge, and it is faithful because any word of edges equals a single edge by filling inner $2$-horns, while a $1$-simplex of a right-pinched mapping space is a $2$-simplex with edges $(\mathrm{id}_x,u,u')$, imposing $u'=u$ in the generated category. By that node an edge has invertible class exactly when it is an equivalence edge. Consequently $B_0$ contains every vertex of $B$; since it is full, it contains every simplex and equals $B$. The supplied inverse is therefore a map $v:B\to A$ with coherent inverse transformations. Conversely, a coherent inverse makes $g$ a functor equivalence; the enhanced-functor calculus then gives weak homotopy equivalences on all its mapping spaces. On homotopy categories the two inverse transformations give $hv\,hg\cong\mathrm{id}$ and $hg\,hv\cong\mathrm{id}$, so $hg$ is essentially surjective. Therefore, for maps between quasicategories, $\mathfrak C[g]$ is Dwyer--Kan exactly when $g$ has a coherent inverse.

source.place: Kerodon Theorem 4.8.4.1 (01JX), via the existing full replete essential-image criterion; the essential-surjectivity hypothesis identifies that full subcategory with the codomain. Reverse implication from the existing functor-equivalence calculus.

proof.text: For maps $g:A\to B$ of quasicategories the testing condition is also equivalent to having a coherent inverse, as follows. If $v$ is such an inverse, precomposition by $v$ is an inverse to precomposition by $g$ on every $h\operatorname{Fun}(-,Z)$: whisker the two inverse transformations to obtain the two natural isomorphisms. Conversely, the test with $Z=A$ supplies $v:B\to A$ and an isomorphism $vg\cong\mathrm{id}_A$ in $h\operatorname{Fun}(A,A)$. Postcomposing gives $gvg\cong g$ in $h\operatorname{Fun}(A,B)$. The test with $Z=B$ says that restriction $h\operatorname{Fun}(B,B)\to h\operatorname{Fun}(A,B)$ is fully faithful; it therefore lifts this isomorphism to $gv\cong\mathrm{id}_B$. These are the coherent inverse transformations: in a quasicategory an isomorphism of objects in its homotopy category is represented by an equivalence edge, by the identification of step 6 and [lem-coef-infinity-mapping-composition], and the functor simplicial sets are quasicategories by the enhanced-functor calculus. The two particular testing categories are allowed in the sufficiently large universe. Combining with step 6 proves the required criterion for $g:A\to B$ between quasicategories.

source.place: HTT Proposition 2.2.5.8, homotopy-category testing; explicit two-test Yoneda argument for quasicategories (agent elaboration)

proof.text: Apply step 7 to the replacement map $f':S'\to T'$ of step 4. In the square $r_T f=f' r_S$, both vertical arrows are categorical equivalences and their coherent realizations are Dwyer--Kan equivalences. Two-out-of-three for categorical equivalences gives that $f$ is a categorical equivalence exactly when $f'$ is. Two-out-of-three for Dwyer--Kan equivalences gives that $\mathfrak C[f]$ is Dwyer--Kan exactly when $\mathfrak C[f']$ is. The equivalence for $f'$ therefore gives the desired equivalence for the original arbitrary simplicial map $f$.
